newsitem.title: egypt: Egypt says peace process in deadlock, not dead end.
newsitem.headline: Egypt says peace process in deadlock, not dead end.

text.p: Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said on Thursday the Middle East peace process had reached a deadlock because of Israel's refusal to stop building settlements but that Arabs would not turn their backs on peace.

The minister was speaking after his second round of talks with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat in as many days on ways to rescue talks that have been stalled since Israel began building a settlement in Arab East Jerusalem on March 18.

"The headline now is 'how to save the peace process'. We see the continuation of settlements as an act of defiance against the Palestinians and the general feeling in the region, and a violation of agreements," Moussa told reporters.
"I can say there is a deadlock but whether we have reached a dead end or not, let's leave this for now, I can't agree with 'dead end'," he added.
Asked about reports that Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak would meet Israeli President Ezer Weizman soon to discuss the crisis in the peace talks, Moussa said:
"President Mubarak called President Weizman yesterday within the framework of contacts agreed upon. There is no meeting between the two presidents during the next few days."

Weizman, an architect of Israel's landmark peace treaty with Egypt while a cabinet minister in 1979, told reporters in Israel that Mubarak proposed in the phone call that they meet in Egypt. An aide to Weizman said they expected a meeting soon.
Arafat did not speak to reporters on Thursday before he left Cairo. He met Mubarak on Wednesday.

Egypt's criticism of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has grown more vocal since work began in March on a new 6,500-home Jewish settlement in Jabal Abu Ghneim, or Har Homa, in East Jerusalem.

Israel occupied East jerusalem during the 1967 Middle East war and later annexed it. The Jewish state claims all of Jerusalem as its undivided capital. Palestinians want the eastern part to be the capital of their future state.
Palestinians see Jewish settlement-building as pre-empting final peace talks on the status of Jerusalem.

Cairo has backed Palestinian demands that Israel halt settlement building before peace talks broken off in March resume. Mubarak has suggested a six-month freeze of the building activity. Netanyahu has said his government will continue settlement building.
Asked if there was hope left for the peace process, despite the distance between the two sides, Moussa replied:

"It's not a question of hope. We must continue with efforts in an active way, not just issue statements but undertake contacts and serious consultations such as today's with President Arafat. The issue is still up for discussion. We can't just leave, close the door and walk away."
Moussa said in remarks published on Thursday that Israel had created the current crisis in the Middle East peace process by wanting to impose a "right-wing, Likud" vision of peace.

"The obstacles we face now, or those faced by the peace process, can be summarised in one sentence: The current Israeli policies want to impose an Israeli peace, a Likud and rightwing peace," Moussa said in an interview in al-Ahram daily.
"It can neither be borne nor accepted. It will lead to the collapse of the foundations of peace itself," he said.
